title: Jacqueline Fernandez Walked Into a Delhi Courtroom Today. The ₹200-Crore Trial She Spent Three Years Avoiding Has Begun.
excerpt: The court found 'strong suspicion' she received ₹5.71 crore in gifts from a convicted conman and moved money to family accounts abroad. Her defense — that she was a victim — was rejected as meritless.
body:
Jacqueline Fernandez walked into a Delhi courtroom today to face what she has spent three years trying to avoid: formal criminal charges in a ₹200-crore money laundering case.

On May 30, Additional Sessions Judge Prashant Sharma of Patiala House Court ordered the framing of charges against Fernandez, alleged conman Sukesh Chandrasekhar, and 15 others. Today — June 3 — the accused were directed to appear physically in court for the formal signing and framing of those charges. The trial, one of Bollywood's most closely watched legal battles, has officially begun.

## The Allegations

The case, investigated by India's Enforcement Directorate, traces back to an elaborate extortion racket allegedly run by Sukesh Chandrasekhar from inside jail. The ED's chargesheet alleges that Fernandez received gifts worth ₹5.71 crore from Chandrasekhar — luxury items, large cash transfers, and expensive possessions — despite knowing of his criminal background.

More damaging for Fernandez: the ED alleges she facilitated the transfer of proceeds of crime to family members abroad. According to the chargesheet, USD 172,913 was transferred to the foreign bank account of her sister Geraldine J. Walker, and AUD 26,740 to the account of her brother Warren J. Fernandez.

The court was blunt in its assessment. "There is prima facie sufficient material on record, raising a strong suspicion that the accused Jacqueline Fernandez committed the offence under Section 3 of PMLA," Judge Sharma stated. The court noted she was "in connivance with Sukesh Chandrasekhar to conceal the use of proceeds of crime."

## Her Defense — and Why the Court Rejected It

Fernandez's legal team has consistently argued that she was an unwitting victim — a woman manipulated by a professional conman who presented himself as someone powerful and connected. Her lawyers contended that she should not be prosecuted under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act since she was never named as an accused in the underlying extortion case registered by Delhi Police.

The court dismissed this argument as meritless, holding that money laundering charges can be brought independently of the underlying scheduled offense. In simpler terms: you don't have to be the person who stole the money to be guilty of laundering it. Receiving and enjoying the proceeds, the court found, is enough.

This is not the first time Fernandez has tried to escape the case through legal channels. In July 2025, the Delhi High Court rejected her petition to quash the ED's proceedings entirely.

## The NRI Dimension

For the Sri Lankan-born, Bahrain-raised actress who made her career in Mumbai, the foreign bank transfers at the heart of this case create an uncomfortable intersection between Bollywood's globalized lifestyle and India's aggressive financial enforcement apparatus.

The ED's case against Fernandez rests heavily on the cross-border movement of money — transfers to accounts in foreign jurisdictions where her family members reside. For NRIs who routinely transfer money between Indian and international accounts, the case raises questions about how Indian financial crime law treats overseas transactions connected to Indian citizens and residents.

The PMLA's extraterritorial reach has been expanding. The Fernandez case, should it result in a conviction, would set a precedent for how Indian courts treat the flow of allegedly tainted funds to accounts held by family members in other countries.

## What Comes Next

With charges now formally framed, the trial moves to the evidentiary phase. Fernandez will either accept or deny the charges — denial is expected — and the ED will begin presenting its witnesses and documentary evidence. Legal observers expect the trial to extend well into 2027.

For Fernandez, who has not announced any new film projects, the courtroom has become her primary public stage. The actress who once commanded ₹5-crore fees per film now faces the possibility of conviction under one of India's most stringent financial crime statutes.

The next hearing date will be set today.
author: Diaspora Desk
